opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. The way I frame it is that a benchmark is really a measuring stick for something you actually care about in the world, and the hard part is making sure the stick measures the right thing. For a long time the field leaned on academic-style evals: multiple-choice questions, math problems, coding puzzles. Those were useful, but models got so good so quickly that a lot of them saturated. You'd see a new benchmark come out and within a year or so models were scoring near the top, and it stopped telling you much.

So one shift for me has been moving toward evals that are grounded in real-world, economically valuable work. Instead of asking "can the model answer this trivia question," you ask "can the model do the kind of task a skilled professional would actually get paid to do?" That might be drafting a legal brief, analyzing a financial model, or putting together a nursing care plan. You bring in experts from those fields to write the tasks and grade the outputs, because they know what good looks like far better than any of us do.

I also care a lot about a few properties. First, the eval has to be hard enough to have headroom, so we can track progress over time instead of hitting a ceiling right away. Second, it should be realistic, closer to the messy, multi-step, context-heavy work people actually do than a clean toy problem. And third, you want grading that's trustworthy, whether that's expert humans, carefully validated model graders, or ideally both.

Benchmarks also matter beyond capability tracking. They're a big part of how we think about safety and preparedness. If you want to know whether a model is getting dangerously good at something, like certain cyber or bio capabilities, you need rigorous evals that tell you that before deployment, not after. So in a way, good evaluation is how we keep ourselves honest, both about how much progress we're making and about what risks come with it.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations should measure whether models can do economically valuable work people actually perform, rather than rely on trivia-style benchmark scores.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about benchmarking is that a benchmark is really a question you're asking the model, and the quality of the answer you get back depends entirely on how carefully you asked it. So the first thing I always want to know is: what is this actually measuring, and does that map onto something that matters in the world?

A lot of early benchmarks were things like multiple-choice trivia or short-answer academic questions. Those were useful for a while, but models saturated them pretty quickly, and once a benchmark is saturated it stops telling you anything. The models get a hundred percent, or close to it, and you can't distinguish between them anymore. So one big part of my job is just staying ahead of that curve, building evaluations that are hard enough that today's frontier models fail, so that the score actually carries information.

The second thing I care about is realism. If I want to know whether a model can do the work of a software engineer, or a research scientist, or a doctor, then the eval should look like that work. That means long tasks, messy inputs, ambiguous instructions, the kind of thing where the model has to figure out what's being asked before it can even start. Those are much harder to build than a set of questions with clean answers, and much harder to grade. You often need expert graders, or rubrics written by people who actually do the job. But I think that difficulty is the point. If a benchmark is easy to construct, it's probably not capturing much.

And the third piece, which I think gets underrated, is contamination and honesty about what a score means. Models are trained on enormous amounts of internet data, so if your test questions are floating around online, you're not measuring capability, you're measuring memorization. So we spend a lot of effort on held-out data, on fresh tasks, on checking whether a model has seen something before. And then when we report a number, we try to be clear about what it does and doesn't tell you. A model scoring well on a coding benchmark doesn't mean it can replace an engineer. It means it did well on the specific slice of engineering we tested.

So the short version is: benchmarks are instruments. You have to keep calibrating them, you have to keep building new ones as the old ones break, and you have to be honest about their limits. When we do that well, they become one of the most useful tools we have for understanding where these systems actually are, and where they're going.

r001.rationale: The candidate says benchmarks should reflect real work and that scores have limits, but it does not clearly prioritize models’ usefulness in people’s real work over benchmark performance as the standard for judging them.

astra-6.text:
I think of a benchmark as a measurement tool, and the first question is: what are you trying to measure? Are you interested in how well a model reasons through a difficult problem, how reliably it follows instructions, or whether it can actually help someone complete a task? Those are different questions, and a single score won’t capture all of them.

A useful benchmark should reflect the situations where you want to use the model. It should also help you understand failures. If a model gets something wrong, was it missing knowledge, misunderstanding the request, or struggling to execute a plan? That distinction matters much more than just knowing that its score went up or down.

So I’d look at benchmarks alongside real-world testing. A benchmark gives you a repeatable way to compare models, and testing with people helps you check whether the improvements you’re measuring translate into something useful.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks should reflect intended use and be paired with real-world testing, but it does not clearly prioritize usefulness in people’s work over benchmark performance as the judging standard.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what are you trying to learn from the benchmark? A model can do really well on a particular set of questions, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how useful it will be for someone doing their actual work.

So I’d start with the tasks people care about, and then ask whether the evaluation captures the conditions under which they’ll use the model. Does it have access to tools? Can it ask clarifying questions? How much time does it have? Those choices can change what you’re measuring quite a bit.

And I’d look beyond a single score. Where does the model fail? Is it consistently good, or does it get something right once and fail the next few times? Benchmarks are useful signals, but the goal is to understand what those signals tell us about real-world performance.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance alone does not show usefulness in actual work and makes real-world tasks and conditions the starting point for evaluation.
